q: Rabies virus belongs to which family and genus?
o: Rhabdoviridae / Lyssavirus
Reoviridae / Orbivirus
Paramyxoviridae / Morbillivirus
Flaviviridae / Flavivirus
e: Rabies virus is the type species of genus Lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae. Flaviviridae contains West Nile and dengue; Paramyxoviridae contains distemper and canine parainfluenza; Reoviridae contains bluetongue.

q: Which structural protein of rabies virus is the primary target for virus-neutralizing antibodies and is the antigen used in all licensed vaccines?
o: Matrix protein (M)
Phosphoprotein (P)
Glycoprotein (G)
Nucleoprotein (N)
e: The G protein is the surface spike glycoprotein that mediates cell entry via acetylcholine receptor and other receptors, and is the dominant neutralizing antigen. All licensed vaccines stimulate anti-G antibody.

q: Why is rabies virus more easily inactivated by common disinfectants than canine parvovirus (CPV)?
o: Rabies virus is smaller than CPV and therefore diffuses out of contaminated surfaces faster
Rabies virus cannot replicate outside a host cell, so it dies within minutes on any surface
Rabies virus is enveloped; its lipid envelope is readily disrupted by soap, bleach, and alcohols
Rabies virus is a DNA virus; DNA is less stable than RNA
e: The lipid envelope is the key. CPV is non-enveloped and persists in the environment for months; RABV is enveloped and is destroyed rapidly by drying, UV, soap, bleach, and alcohols. This distinction is a classic exam trap.

q: A dog is bitten on the left hind foot by a raccoon. Which of the following best explains why this dog would be expected to have a longer incubation period than a dog bitten on the face?
o: Virus must travel a longer distance via retrograde axoplasmic transport to reach the spinal cord and brain
The hind limb has fewer blood vessels to carry virus to the CNS
The hind limb has thicker skin, reducing initial viral inoculation
The hind limb has fewer lymphatics to amplify the initial infection
e: RABV travels centripetally via retrograde axoplasmic transport at ~50–100 mm/day. A bite on the foot requires transport across the entire hind limb and spinal cord before reaching the brain, whereas a facial bite is centimeters from the brainstem.

q: What is the significance of the centrifugal phase of rabies virus spread in the context of ante-mortem diagnosis?
o: It means virus can be isolated from blood in the viremic phase
It causes the animal to shed virus in feces, enabling environmental surveillance
Virus spreads to salivary glands and nuchal skin, enabling ante-mortem detection by RT-PCR on saliva or skin biopsy
It allows serology to become positive before clinical signs
e: Once RABV reaches the brain, it spreads centrifugally to peripheral organs including salivary glands and skin hair follicles. This makes ante-mortem RT-PCR on saliva or nuchal skin biopsy possible in humans suspected of having rabies.

q: Which eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion body is pathognomonic for rabies encephalitis, and in which location is it most reliably found?
o: Cowdry Type A bodies; in hepatocytes
Bollinger bodies; in epithelial cells of the skin
Lewy bodies; in the substantia nigra
Negri bodies; most reliably in hippocampal neurons and cerebellar Purkinje cells
e: Negri bodies are pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusions in infected neurons. They are most reliably found in the hippocampus (Ammon's horn) and cerebellar Purkinje cells. However, they are absent in ~20–30% of confirmed cases, so the DFA test is the gold standard, not histopathology.

q: A shelter receives a stray dog showing sudden jaw drop, drooling, and an inability to eat or drink. A technician opens the dog's mouth to examine for a foreign body. What is the most important concern?
o: Aspiration pneumonia from drooling
Rabies — pharyngeal paralysis is a sign of the paralytic form; the technician may have had an unprotected exposure
Botulism — treatment with antitoxin should start immediately
Tetanus causing masseter spasm
e: Jaw drop with hypersalivation and dysphagia in a stray animal is a classic presentation of the paralytic ("dumb") form of rabies. Examining the mouth without PPE constitutes a potential mucous membrane or wound exposure to saliva. Rabies must be considered before any unprotected examination.

q: A rabies-suspect animal must be euthanized and its brain submitted for DFA testing. Which euthanasia method is CONTRAINDICATED?
o: Inhalant anesthetic overdose followed by IV pentobarbital
IV pentobarbital overdose
IC pentobarbital under deep general anesthesia
Gunshot to the head
e: Gunshot to the head destroys the brainstem, cerebellum, and hippocampus — the tissue required for DFA testing. This renders the specimen non-diagnostic. Any method that preserves brain architecture (IV barbiturate overdose, deep anesthesia followed by IC injection) is appropriate.

q: The 10-day observation rule applies to which three domestic species after a bite incident?
o: Dogs, ferrets, and horses
Dogs, cats, and rabbits
Dogs, cats, and ferrets
Dogs, cats, and guinea pigs
e: Dogs, cats, and ferrets are the only domestic species for which the pre-clinical shedding window is well established and the 10-day observation rule applies. Rabbits, guinea pigs, and horses are not covered by the 10-day rule.

q: A currently vaccinated dog is bitten by a stray cat that tests positive for rabies. Per NASPHV Compendium recommendations, what is the appropriate management of the dog?
o: Revaccinate immediately and place under 45-day observation
4-month (120-day) strict isolation quarantine
10-day home observation with no further action
Immediate euthanasia and DFA testing
e: A currently vaccinated animal exposed to a confirmed or probable rabid animal should be revaccinated immediately and observed for 45 days. The strict isolation quarantine (4 months / 120 days for dogs and cats; 6 months for ferrets, NASPHV 2016) is for unvaccinated exposed animals whose owners choose not to elect euthanasia — not for this currently-vaccinated dog. The 10-day rule applies to biting incidents involving domestic animals and humans, not to animal-animal exposures.

q: A bat is found in a room where a child was sleeping alone. The child has no visible bite marks. What is the recommended course of action?
o: No action needed; bat bites always leave visible marks
Test the bat; PEP is only required if the bat tests positive
Observe the child for 10 days before deciding on PEP
Capture the bat for testing and initiate PEP unless the bat tests negative; a sleeping child cannot reliably report a bite
e: Bat bites are often imperceptible. A bat in the room with a sleeping person, an unattended child, or an intoxicated person is a PEP indication in most jurisdictions because the person cannot reliably confirm or deny a bite. PEP should be initiated unless the bat can be tested and tests negative.

q: Which of the following contacts with a rabies-suspect animal does NOT constitute a rabies exposure requiring PEP evaluation?
o: The handler is bitten through thin latex gloves
Saliva contacts the handler's conjunctiva while the animal is being restrained
The handler touches the animal's fur with intact skin on both hands
Saliva from the animal contacts an open wound on the handler's hand
e: Intact skin contact does not constitute a rabies exposure. Exposures require virus contact with broken skin or mucous membranes. Bites through thin gloves, saliva on open wounds, and saliva on mucous membranes are all exposures requiring evaluation.

q: An unvaccinated person is bitten by a bat. What is the correct administration of rabies immune globulin (RIG)?
o: 20 IU/kg dose given IM on day 0 and again on day 3
As much of the 20 IU/kg dose as anatomically feasible infiltrated into and around the wound; remainder given IM at a distant site on day 0
20 IU/kg dose given IV over 30 minutes on day 0
Entire 20 IU/kg dose given IM in the deltoid on day 0
e: RIG must be infiltrated into and around the wound to neutralize virus at the inoculation site. Any remainder is given IM at a site distant from vaccine administration. It is given only on day 0; giving it after day 7 can blunt the vaccine response. It is not given IV and not repeated.

q: A shelter veterinarian who completed the 3-dose pre-exposure prophylaxis series 3 years ago and has confirmed adequate antibody titres is bitten by a suspected-rabid raccoon. What is the correct PEP protocol?
o: Full 4-dose vaccine series plus RIG
No PEP needed; pre-exposure vaccination is fully protective
RIG only; no vaccine needed because of prior vaccination
2 doses of vaccine on days 0 and 3; no RIG
e: Previously vaccinated individuals (prior complete pre-exposure series or prior PEP with demonstrated antibody response) receive only 2 booster doses of vaccine (days 0 and 3) and no RIG. RIG can actually suppress the anamnestic immune response in pre-vaccinated individuals and is contraindicated.

q: Which of the following is true regarding 1-year vs. 3-year veterinary rabies vaccines?
o: Both products are immunologically equivalent; the difference is the USDA-approved label duration
3-year vaccines contain higher antigen mass and provide superior immunity
1-year vaccines are modified-live; 3-year vaccines are killed
3-year vaccines must be given with adjuvant; 1-year vaccines may be non-adjuvanted
e: The duration designation is a regulatory distinction based on challenge studies conducted to obtain the specific label claim. The vaccines are immunologically equivalent; using a 1-year product does not provide inferior protection per dose. However, for legal and public health purposes an animal vaccinated with a 1-year product must be revaccinated annually to remain "currently vaccinated."

q: Which of the following best describes the reason a recombinant (canarypox-vectored) rabies vaccine is preferred over an adjuvanted killed vaccine in cats?
o: Recombinant vaccines provide longer duration of immunity (5 years) in cats
Adjuvanted vaccines are not licensed for use in cats in the US
Adjuvanted vaccines have a higher (though still rare) association with feline injection-site sarcoma; recombinant vaccines are non-adjuvanted, reducing this risk
Recombinant vaccines elicit superior cell-mediated immunity in cats compared with killed products
e: Feline injection-site sarcoma (FISS) is associated with adjuvanted vaccines (and other injected products). Recombinant rabies vaccines (e.g., canarypox-vectored) are non-adjuvanted and are therefore preferred by current AAFP vaccine guidelines to reduce FISS risk. Duration of immunity under the label is 1–3 years depending on product.

q: Which domestic animal species is currently the most frequently reported rabid domestic animal in the United States?
o: Dogs
Horses
Cats
Cattle
e: Cats surpassed dogs as the most commonly reported rabid domestic animal in the US, largely because vaccination rates in cats (especially free-roaming cats) lag behind those in dogs, and some jurisdictions do not legally mandate cat vaccination. This is a high-frequency exam fact.

q: A shelter staff member is bitten by an impounded stray dog of unknown vaccination status. The dog is available for observation. What is the immediate first step?
o: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, then report to a supervisor and seek medical evaluation / public health consultation
Euthanize the dog and submit brain for DFA testing
Place the dog under 10-day observation and take no further action regarding the staff member
Begin PEP immediately without waiting for public health consultation
e: Immediate thorough wound washing is the single most important first step — it significantly reduces viral inoculation. Then report and seek medical/public health evaluation. The decision about PEP is made in consultation with the health department. Euthanasia is not required if the animal is available for 10-day observation.

q: The NASPHV Compendium of Animal Rabies Prevention and Control is best described as:
o: The authoritative national reference for vaccine schedules, quarantine periods, and exposure management, published by the National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians and updated periodically
A federal regulation that overrides state law in all US jurisdictions
A document published by the CDC that is legally binding for animal control agencies
An AVMA policy statement that applies only to licensed veterinarians
e: The NASPHV Compendium is an evidence-based, nationally recognized reference document but is not a federal regulation. States and localities may adopt its recommendations into law or exceed its standards. Veterinarians and shelter staff should follow the Compendium's guidance and local law, whichever is more stringent.

q: From a One Health perspective, which single intervention has been shown to be most cost-effective for preventing human rabies deaths globally?
o: Oral rabies vaccination of raccoon and skunk populations in North America
Achieving and sustaining ≥70% vaccination coverage in the domestic dog population
Mandatory rabies vaccination of all cats in the United States
Expanding access to human PEP in low-income countries
e: Dogs are the reservoir responsible for >99% of human rabies deaths globally. Mathematical modeling and field evidence consistently show that achieving ≥70% vaccination coverage in domestic dogs breaks transmission chains and is more cost-effective than PEP availability alone. This is the foundation of the WHO/FAO/WOAH Zero by 30 strategy.

q: How did the median price owners were willing to pay compare with the actual cost of vaccination?
o: It exceeded the actual cost
It was less than the actual cost
Owners refused to pay anything
It equaled the actual cost
e: Willingness-to-pay (median ~25 birr) was below the real cost, supporting the need for subsidized or free vaccine.

q: What vaccination coverage threshold is cited as needed for canine rabies elimination?
e: The 70% coverage threshold is the stated target for canine rabies elimination.

q: Which delivery strategy did results support incorporating to maximize coverage?
o: Central-point clinics only
Mandatory quarantine
Online registration only
Door-to-door vaccination plus subsidies
e: Many owners were unwilling to travel, so door-to-door vaccination combined with subsidies was endorsed.

q: A 2016 cross-sectional survey of 123 dog-owning households in Mahajanga, Madagascar assessed rabies vaccination coverage and dog ecology. What proportion of owned dogs had been vaccinated against rabies?
o: Approximately 95%
Approximately 56%
Approximately 84%
Approximately 34%
e: Only about one third (34%) of owned dogs were vaccinated against rabies, despite most dogs being owner-accessible for preventive vaccination.

q: What were the main owner-cited obstacles to dog rabies vaccination?
o: Belief that dogs cannot transmit rabies
Lack of vaccine supply and government bans
Vaccine safety fears and religious beliefs
Limited finances and poor access to veterinary care
e: Owners cited limited financial resources and difficulty accessing veterinary services as the chief barriers.

q: What did the authors conclude about the accessibility of dogs for preventive vaccination?
o: Most dogs were accessible through their owners
Vaccination should target only stray dogs
Vaccination is unnecessary given low rabies risk
Most dogs were ownerless and unreachable
e: Most dogs were owned and thus reachable for vaccination, yet coverage remained low.

q: Which wildlife species accounted for the most US rabies cases in 2021?
o: Skunks
Raccoons
Foxes
Bats
e: Bats were the leading rabid host at 33.9% of cases.

q: Among domestic animals, which had the most reported rabies cases in 2021?
o: Cats
Dogs
Horses
Cattle
e: Cats (216 cases) led domestic animal rabies, exceeding cattle and dogs.

q: How did total US animal rabies cases in 2021 compare with 2020?
o: 18.2% decrease
18% increase
Roughly unchanged
Doubled
e: Cases fell 18.2% from 4,479 (2020) to 3,663 (2021), attributed to pandemic factors.

q: A US analysis of dog import data from 2015 to 2022 estimated the rabies incidence in dogs imported from dog-mediated rabies virus variant (DMRVV)-enzootic countries, compared to domestically acquired rabies in the general US dog population, to be approximately:
o: 16 times higher
About the same
100 times higher
Half as high
e: The estimated incidence rate of rabies was 16 times higher (range 13.2–19.4) in dogs imported from DMRVV-enzootic countries than in the domestic US dog population.

q: Per the abstract, dog-mediated rabies virus variant has been eliminated from the United States since:
e: The abstract states DMRVV has been eliminated from the US since 2007.

q: A study analyzing US dog imports (2015–2022) found that dogs from countries with dog-mediated rabies virus variant (DMRVV) carried a substantially higher rabies risk than domestic US dogs. This finding supports:
o: Importation requirements to prevent reintroduction of dog-mediated rabies virus variant (DMRVV) into the United States
Mandatory desexing of imported dogs
Eliminating domestic rabies vaccination
Banning all dog adoption
e: The higher rabies risk in dogs from DMRVV-enzootic countries supports importation requirements aimed at preventing DMRVV reintroduction into the United States.

q: In the Philippine survey, the human-to-dog ratio yielded the most dogs per 1000 people in which setting?
o: Urban areas
Semi-urban areas
Rural areas
Small islands
e: Rural areas had 256.3 dogs/1000 people, the highest of all settings.

q: After adjusting targets and resources using survey data in Quezon City and Cebu City, what happened to rabies vaccination?
o: A modest 10% rise
A 3- to 4-fold increase in dogs vaccinated
No measurable change
Coverage declined
e: Data-driven adjustments produced a 3- to 4-fold increase in dogs vaccinated versus previous years.

q: The study estimated the total Philippine dog population at approximately:
o: 10 million
23 million
2 million
50 million
e: The estimate was 23.29 million dogs (95% CI 22.51–24.07 million).

q: How does seeking Hadkai Mata faith healing affect conventional rabies care?
o: It replaces vaccination entirely
It accelerates hospital referral
It is actively forbidden by healers
Post-exposure prophylaxis is often delayed while traditional treatment is sought first
e: PEP is not opposed per se but is frequently delayed because patients try traditional treatment first.

q: What attitude toward mass dog vaccination did the study find among worshippers?
o: Strong endorsement
Demand for more vaccine
Reluctance, viewing it as interfering with the goddess's control of dogs
Indifference
e: Some reluctance arose because vaccination was seen as interfering with how the goddess controls/enrages dogs.

q: The paper's main strategic conclusion for rabies control in this region is to:
o: Rely solely on biomedical messaging
Ban temple worship
Cull stray dogs
Use multidisciplinary approaches addressing cultural perceptions
e: It highlights multidisciplinary, culturally tailored approaches as critical to effective rabies control.

q: What 'One Medicine' strategy do the authors propose to accelerate rabies therapy development?
o: Investigational treatment of naturally infected dogs receiving human-like supportive care
Mass human vaccine trials
Abandoning treatment research
Computer modeling only
e: They propose treating naturally infected dogs under conditions mimicking the human scenario to study combination therapies.

q: How many categories of disease process do the authors say must be managed in rabies patients?
o: Eight
Six
Four
Two
e: Four: viral propagation, neuronal degeneration, inflammation, and systemic compromise.

q: What is the stated current prognosis for human rabies patients?
o: Generally favorable with PEP
Dire, with little treatment progress
Fully curable with antivirals
Self-limiting
e: The abstract states the prognosis for recovery remains dire and little treatment progress has been made.

q: Into which three categories did the study group barriers to dog vaccination in Chad?
o: Economic, socio-cultural, institutional
Genetic, clinical, surgical
Legal, financial, military
Urban, rural, nomadic
e: Barriers were grouped into economic, socio-cultural, and institutional levels.

q: Which was identified as a socio-cultural barrier to dog vaccination?
o: High literacy among owners
Belief that vaccine harms dog-meat's therapeutic properties and that dogs are impure in Muslim faith
Government subsidies
Excess vaccine supply
e: Cited socio-cultural barriers included the dog-meat therapeutic-property belief and dogs being considered impure in Muslim faith.

q: What proportion of human rabies cases worldwide do domestic dogs account for, per the abstract?
e: Domestic dogs are responsible for 95% of all human rabies cases worldwide.

q: A novel country-infrastructure index called STOP-R was developed to estimate dog-mediated rabies elimination capacity. It is built from which type of data?
o: Direct laboratory surveillance case counts
Country-level infrastructure indicators (literacy, infant mortality, electricity access, political stability, natural hazards)
Canine vaccine antibody titers
Genetic sequences of rabies virus variants
e: The STOP-R index was built from five publicly available country-level infrastructure indicators, not direct laboratory surveillance.

q: Using a country-infrastructure index for rabies burden estimation, projected global human deaths from dog-mediated rabies virus variant (DMRVV) in endemic countries from 2022 to 2030 are expected to:
o: Increase sharply
Decrease
Double
Stay unchanged
e: Estimates fall from approximately 40,111 in 2022 to approximately 32,349 in 2030.

q: A study that developed a country-infrastructure index (STOP-R) to estimate dog-mediated rabies elimination capacity concluded that success in eliminating dog-mediated rabies is:
o: Unrelated to country infrastructure
Determined solely by vaccine coverage
Influenced by factors external to rabies programs such as country infrastructure
Independent of political stability
e: The STOP-R study concluded that factors external to specific rabies programs — particularly country-level infrastructure — influence elimination progress.

q: Across the 70 included studies, dog rabies-vaccination uptake ranged how widely?
o: Always below 10%
From less than 1% to over 90%, with none reaching full coverage
Consistently above 70%
Uniformly near 50%
e: Uptake ranged from <1% to >90% with no study reporting full coverage.

q: In a 2025 global scoping review of dog owners' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding rabies prevention (70 studies, 2012–2025), which factor showed a strong positive correlation (r = 0.69, p = 0.004) with vaccination practice?
o: Dog body size
Pet age
Owner awareness of vaccine benefits
Urban residence
e: Across studies included in this KAP scoping review, owner awareness of vaccine benefits correlated strongly (r = 0.69, p = 0.004) with vaccination practice, underscoring targeted communication as a key lever for improving coverage.

q: A 2025 global scoping review of dog owner knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) for rabies control (70 studies, 2012–2025) identified which common barriers to dog vaccination?
o: Fear of microchips
Lack of information, vaccine accessibility, and distance to clinics
Religious objection only
Excessive free clinics
e: The scoping review identified lack of information, vaccine accessibility, distance to clinics, and personal constraints as the common barriers to vaccination across the included studies.

q: Which clinical presentation split is the classic teaching pattern for rabies in dogs versus cats?
o: Dogs more often show the furious form; cats more often show the paralytic (dumb) form
Dogs more often progress to the paralytic (dumb) form; cats more often show the furious form
Only dogs can show the furious form
Only cats can show the paralytic form
e: Either species can show either presentation, but dogs are classically associated with progressing to the paralytic (dumb) form and cats with the furious form.

q: The direct rapid immunohistochemical test (DRIT/dRIT) for postmortem rabies diagnosis is best described as:
o: An antemortem serum antibody test used to confirm vaccination
A postmortem brain-tissue test read on a standard light microscope, with sensitivity and specificity comparable to DFA in validation studies
A test that replaces the need for a fresh, unfixed brain sample
A screening test performed on saliva or blood
e: DRIT is a postmortem brain-tissue test that does not require a fluorescence microscope. In one 2025 dog-brain-sample study it matched DFA at 100% sensitivity and specificity, alongside a lateral flow assay and RT-PCR.

q: A shelter veterinarian is collecting a brain sample from a suspect-rabid animal for DFA/DRIT testing. What is the key precaution during sample collection?
o: Freeze the whole head immediately before shipping to the lab
Avoid using a saw to open the skull, since mechanical sectioning can aerosolize infectious material; submit the refrigerated whole head for controlled removal instead
Use a saw but only if wearing a surgical mask
No special precaution is needed, since rabies virus is highly resistant to disinfection
e: Sawing bone/brain tissue risks aerosolizing rabies virus; the safer approach is to refrigerate (not freeze) and ship the whole head so the lab can perform controlled tissue removal. Rabies virus is actually enveloped and easily inactivated by routine disinfectants — the aerosol risk is specific to mechanical sectioning, not general handling.

q: Regarding the age at which the first rabies dose is given, which statement is most accurate?
o: It must always be given at exactly 6 months of age
It usually starts at 3 months (12 weeks) of age, and most jurisdictions mandate that it be given no later than 4 months (16 weeks) of age
There is no upper age limit for the first dose in any jurisdiction
It cannot legally be given before 6 months of age anywhere in the US
e: Label minimums are commonly 12 or 16 weeks, and most jurisdictions require the first dose by 4 months of age at the latest.

q: A stray dog has a high rabies antibody titer but no vaccination record. For regulatory purposes (quarantine classification, legal compliance, travel/import), this animal is treated as:
o: Fully vaccinated, since the titer proves protective immunity
Unvaccinated — a titer is not proof of vaccination status and cannot substitute for a documented vaccine history
Exempt from future vaccination requirements
Vaccinated only for travel purposes, but not for quarantine purposes
e: Regulatory determinations require a valid vaccination certificate; a titer, however high, does not substitute for documented vaccination.

q: A person handles a raccoon oral rabies vaccine (ORV) bait without gloves. How does this compare to exposure to a standard parenteral (injectable) rabies vaccine?
o: Both require identical reporting to public health/wildlife officials
ORV bait exposure must be reported, because the bait contains a live-vectored vaccine virus; parenteral vaccine exposure does not carry this reporting requirement
Neither exposure requires reporting
Only parenteral vaccine exposure requires reporting
e: ORV baits contain a live-vectored vaccine virus, so contact or ingestion should be reported to public health/wildlife officials; routine parenteral vaccine handling does not require this.

q: Community cats vaccinated for rabies at the time of TNR (trap-neuter-return) surgery, without any booster, typically maintain protective antibody titers for approximately:
o: 2 to 4 weeks
3 to 4 months
3 to 4 years
10 to 15 years
e: TNR-vaccinated community cats commonly maintain protective titers for roughly 3 to 4 years without a booster, which underlies the single-vaccination-at-surgery model most TNR programs use.

q: A rescue is arranging interstate transport of a dog that is not currently vaccinated against rabies and originates from a rabies-endemic country, including a batch moving as part of a TNR partner program. What is required?
o: A same-day USDA health certificate with no further paperwork
A USDA health certificate plus an import permit applied for at least 10 days before travel, with additional paperwork; the same rule applies to the TNR transport
Nothing extra, since TNR-program transports are exempt from import rules
Only a rabies antibody titer result
e: Unvaccinated or endemic-area animals require an import permit applied for at least 10 days ahead, in addition to the standard health certificate, and TNR/community-cat transports are not exempt from this rule.

q: What is a shelter's public-health responsibility to an adopter regarding rabies at the point of adoption?
o: None — rabies status is the adopter's responsibility to research independently
Communicate the animal's current vaccination status, the legal revaccination timeline, and that a titer cannot substitute for documented vaccination, as part of standard adoption counseling
Provide this information only if the adopter specifically asks
Provide a titer result in place of a vaccination certificate
e: Shelters carry a public-health duty to proactively communicate rabies vaccination status and the legal revaccination timeline to adopters, not wait to be asked.

q: In a 2025 prospective study, kittens averaging ~9 weeks old with pre-vaccination rabies titers below the susceptible threshold (<0.1 IU/mL) were given a single rabies vaccine below the standard label age. What happened at the 28-day recheck?
o: None of the kittens mounted a protective titer
Only kittens over 12 weeks responded protectively
All 10 enrolled kittens mounted a protective response (>0.5 IU/mL)
Titers were protective at 28 days but had waned to nonprotective by 12 weeks
e: All 10 kittens, susceptible pre-vaccination with no measurable maternal antibody, mounted a protective antibody response (>0.5 IU/mL) 28 days after a single rabies vaccine given below the standard label age — supporting vaccination at the time of surgical sterilization once MDA has cleared.

q: According to the US National Rabies Surveillance System's 2023 report, the large majority of animal rabies cases reported were in wildlife rather than domestic animals. Among domestic animals, which species was most frequently found to be rabid?
o: Dogs, reflecting continued sylvatic rabies spillover into unvaccinated pet populations
Cats, which were the domestic animal species most frequently diagnosed with rabies in 2023
Cattle, due to frequent exposure to rabid wildlife in pastured settings
Horses, which accounted for the majority of the 309 domestic animal rabies cases
e: Of the 3,760 animal rabies cases reported in the US in 2023, only 309 (8.2%) were in domestic animals, with the remaining 91.8% in wildlife. Among domestic animals, cats (222 cases) were the most frequently diagnosed rabid species, while bats (1,298 cases) and raccoons (1,085 cases) were the most frequently found rabid wildlife. No human rabies cases were reported in the US, Canada, or Mexico in 2023.

q: Analysis of the CDC's National Rabies Surveillance System data from 2002 to 2022 found that true rabies vaccine failures in dogs and cats were which of the following?
o: Common, occurring in more than 20% of vaccinated animals subsequently exposed to rabies

Rare; vaccinated dogs and cats were more than 90-fold less likely to contract rabies than unvaccinated animals, and current vaccination practices are projected to prevent substantial public health and healthcare costs
Essentially nonexistent, as no vaccinated animal in the surveillance system tested positive for rabies during the study period
Increasing steadily over the 20-year study period, suggesting declining vaccine efficacy
e: Over the 20-year study period, only 15 true rabies vaccine failures (11 dogs and 4 cats) were identified among documented cases, a small fraction of the rabid animals reported. Up-to-date vaccination made dogs and cats 130.8 and 93.6 times less likely, respectively, to contract rabies compared with nonvaccinated animals. Current vaccination practices were projected to prevent about $166 million in public health- and healthcare-related costs over the following 10 years.

q: A survey of veterinary professionals serving as representatives of local communities in Turkana County, Kenya, assessed community knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding dog rabies. What did the results indicate?
o: The majority of the community was knowledgeable about rabies and could recognize clinical signs in dogs
Cost was not a barrier to vaccination; vaccine unavailability was the primary obstacle
Veterinary professionals reported no meaningful gaps in community rabies knowledge across sub-counties

Community knowledge, positive attitudes, and practices regarding rabies and dog vaccination were rated below 50% across the region, with insufficient awareness, lack of information about campaigns, and cost cited as key barriers to vaccination
e: 42.4% of surveyed veterinary professionals believed less than half the community was knowledgeable about rabies, and 75.8% thought less than half could recognize clinical signs in dogs; knowledge, positive attitudes, and practices around dog vaccination were similarly rated below 50%. The main barriers to vaccination identified were insufficient awareness, lack of information about immunization campaigns, and cost. The study concluded that rabies-related KAP was unsatisfactory across all sub-counties.

q: Evaluation of mass dog rabies vaccination campaigns in rural (Itezhi tezhi) and urban (Lusaka) communities in Zambia found which outcome?
o: The 70% herd immunity threshold was achieved in both the rural and urban campaigns
Rural campaigns consistently failed to reach adequate coverage while the urban campaign exceeded its target
Dog population density showed no relationship with human population density

The urban (Lusaka) campaign failed to reach the 70% herd immunity threshold, partly due to challenges in community sensitization and travel distance to central vaccination points, while the large majority of Zambia's dogs actually reside in low-density rural areas
e: Herd immunity (70% coverage) was not achieved in the urban Lusaka campaign, likely due to challenges with pre-campaign community sensitization and travel distance to the central vaccination points used. Dog population density correlated strongly with human population density; extrapolating nationally suggested about 3.2 million dogs in Zambia, with 86% residing in low-density rural communities. Prioritizing higher-density dog populations could improve campaign effectiveness.
